lessons.title: What ovarian reserve testing measures
lessons.objective: Tell oocyte quantity apart from reproductive potential and know what AMH and AFC are useful for in stimulation.
lessons.closing: AMH and AFC count; they are not good independent predictors of pregnancy. Their territory is anticipating how many oocytes will respond to stimulation.

lessons.title: AMH and natural fertility
lessons.objective: Interpret the evidence that AMH does not predict spontaneous conception and explain it to patients.
lessons.closing: In women without known infertility, a low AMH did not foretell fewer conceptions (positive test). Ordering it “to know whether I can wait” does not answer that question.

lessons.title: Responsible use: don't deny, don't sell, don't over-order
lessons.objective: Avoid inappropriate uses of reserve markers: denying treatment, promoting egg freezing and ordering obsolete dynamic tests.
lessons.closing: A lab number guides counselling; on its own it does not decide who gets treatment or who freezes eggs.

items.title: AMH and AFC measure quantity, not quality
items.core: Ovarian reserve markers estimate how many follicles remain; their relation to oocyte quality and live birth is weak or inconsistent. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
The antral follicle count (AFC) is the sum of antral follicles in both ovaries on transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase; most studies define them as 2–10 mm in mean diameter. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

AMH is produced by granulosa cells of growing follicles, so it tracks the size of the follicle pool. Neither marker tells you about the competence of each oocyte.
items.recall: What does AMH tell you, and what doesn't it?

rows.text: Oocyte quality and live birth: weak or inconsistent relation

visual.alt: Diagram: AMH and AFC reflect follicle number; their relation to oocyte quality and live birth is weak or inconsistent.

items.application: When reporting an AMH, explicitly separate “how many” from “how good”: it is a common confusion.

items.title: Before interpreting an AMH: what changes it
items.core: AMH may be suppressed by current or recent combined hormonal contraception and by ovarian surgery, and it varies with age, BMI and cycle day. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
According to the practice points of the 2023 international PCOS guideline: in the general population AMH peaks around ages 20–25 and is lower with higher BMI; it may be suppressed by current or recent combined contraception and by ovarian surgery; and it may vary across the cycle. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

Laboratories should use population- and assay-specific cut-offs: an AMH that is “low by the lab range” cannot be compared directly with figures from another assay. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Which factors can lower or alter an AMH, and what should you check about the lab?
items.application: Before interpreting an AMH, ask about recent hormonal contraception and ovarian surgery, and check which assay and cut-off the lab used.

items.title: What they are for: predicting response to stimulation
items.core: ESHRE recommends using AFC or AMH to predict a high or low response to ovarian stimulation. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.body:
Reserve markers are good predictors of the number of oocytes retrieved in IVF. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

By contrast, the ESHRE guideline advises against routinely using age, BMI, basal FSH, inhibin B, oestradiol, progesterone or basal LH to predict response. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]] In short: to anticipate response, AFC or AMH; not a panel of basal hormones.
items.recall: Which marker does ESHRE recommend to predict response to stimulation?
items.application: If a patient is going to stimulation, AMH or AFC help anticipate low or high response and counsel on risks; adding inhibin B or FSH is not needed for that.
items.pearl: AFC or AMH, depending on context: ESHRE recommends either one to stratify response. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]

items.title: Myth: “low AMH = IVF won't work”
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend AFC, AMH or other basal markers to predict pregnancy or live birth; female age and BMI, by contrast, are predictors. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.body:
According to ASRM, AMH as an independent variable is at best weakly predictive of pregnancy. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

NICE takes a different nuance: it recommends using AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] This is not a head-on contradiction: fewer oocytes means fewer cumulative opportunities, but it does not say which will be competent and does not mean “it won’t work”.
items.recall: Is AMH useful to forecast live birth in IVF?
items.pearl: Always distinguish the outcome: oocytes retrieved (biomarker) ≠ clinical pregnancy ≠ live birth.

items.title: Key study: low AMH did not predict fewer conceptions
items.core: In women aged 30–44 without known infertility, AMH <0.7 ng/mL was not associated with a lower probability of conceiving by 6 or 12 cycles. [[ref:steiner-2017-jama]]
items.body:
Prospective cohort: 981 women enrolled and 750 analysed, trying to conceive for ≤3 months. Adjusted probability of conceiving with AMH <0.7 ng/mL versus normal AMH: 65% vs 62% by 6 cycles and 84% vs 75% by 12 cycles, with no significant differences. The low-AMH subgroup was small (84 women) and its confidence interval wide (50–75% by 6 cycles). High FSH was not associated with lower fertility either. [[ref:steiner-2017-jama]]

Mind the outcome: “conception” was a positive pregnancy test, not a live birth. And it does not apply to women with already diagnosed infertility.
items.recall: What did Steiner 2017 find about low AMH and the chance of conceiving?

visual.alt: Adjusted probability of conceiving with AMH below 0.7 ng/mL versus normal: 65% versus 62% by 6 cycles and 84% versus 75% by 12 cycles; no significant difference.

items.application: Useful to reassure, with data, a woman without infertility who brings a low AMH from a check-up; reassurance does not change the weight of age or time trying.

evidence.label: association
evidence.note: Prospective cohort: association, not a trial.

items.title: What I would not order: reserve testing to forecast spontaneous pregnancy
items.core: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the cause of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
It is a strong ESHRE recommendation with low certainty of evidence: strength and certainty are different things. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

ASRM agrees: the markers do not predict current reproductive potential in women of unproven fertility, and in women with infertility they are not useful to predict unassisted pregnancy. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]] NICE concurs: do not use AMH to predict pregnancy through spontaneous conception. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: In a woman with regular cycles, is AMH needed to work up the cause of her infertility?
items.pearl: A recommendation can be strong even with low-certainty evidence when the balance of benefit, harm and cost is clear.

items.title: Patient phrase: “Does my AMH tell me if I can wait?”
items.core: Reserve markers should not be used as a fertility test. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
Suggested answer: “AMH estimates how many eggs would respond to treatment, but it does not predict when you will get pregnant or whether you can wait. In women without fertility problems, a low AMH was not associated with fewer pregnancies.” [[ref:steiner-2017-jama]]

Then discuss what does matter for her plan: age, time trying, cycles, history and assessment of the partner.
items.recall: How would you explain to a patient what her AMH can and cannot tell her?
items.application: Prevents an isolated number from causing distress or rushed decisions.

items.title: A very low AMH does not justify refusing IVF
items.core: Extremely low AMH values should not be used to refuse IVF treatment. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
ASRM is explicit: reserve markers should not be used to deny access to infertility treatment. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

They do help with counselling: with very low reserve fewer oocytes are expected, and that information supports shared decisions about expectations and alternatives.
items.recall: Can a very low AMH alone be a reason to refuse IVF?

items.title: Don't use AMH to promote egg freezing
items.core: Ovarian reserve markers should not be used to promote planned oocyte cryopreservation. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
The reasoning follows from the above: if AMH does not predict current reproductive potential, it cannot indicate who “needs” to freeze. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

The decision to freeze is discussed from the person's reproductive plans and realistic information about the technique, not from a lab value used as an alarm.
items.recall: Should a low AMH be used to recommend egg freezing?

items.title: Tests to drop: clomiphene challenge and isolated FSH
items.core: Dynamic tests such as the clomiphene citrate challenge test do not improve prediction of poor response over basal markers and should be abandoned. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]
items.body:
An elevated basal FSH is specific but not sensitive for diminished ovarian reserve: if high it is informative, but a normal FSH does not rule it out. [[ref:asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve]]

That is why, when reserve truly needs estimating (for example, before stimulation), AFC or AMH are preferred. [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.recall: What is the limitation of a normal basal FSH for ruling out low reserve?

items.stem: Which of these outcomes does AMH predict best?

options.text: The number of oocytes retrieved in IVF stimulation.
options.why: Correct: reserve markers are good predictors of oocyte yield.

options.text: The probability of live birth after IVF.
options.why: AMH is at best weakly predictive of pregnancy; ESHRE advises against using it to predict live birth.

options.text: The probability of spontaneous pregnancy within 6 months.
options.why: In women without infertility, a low AMH was not associated with a lower chance of conceiving.

options.text: The quality of each oocyte.
options.why: AMH reflects quantity; its association with oocyte quality is weak.

items.explanation: AMH and AFC count follicles: their strength is anticipating how many oocytes will be retrieved.

items.stem: Before IVF stimulation, what does ESHRE recommend to predict a high or low response?

options.text: Basal inhibin B.
options.why: ESHRE lists it among markers not to be routinely used to predict response.

options.text: AFC or AMH.
options.why: Correct: this is the ESHRE guideline recommendation.

options.text: Combined basal FSH and oestradiol.
options.why: Both are among the markers ESHRE advises against routinely using to predict response.

options.text: Age and BMI.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend routinely using them to predict ovarian response.

items.explanation: To anticipate response: AFC or AMH. Not a panel of basal hormones.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman, trying to conceive for 2 months, regular cycles, no history. She brings a low AMH from a check-up. Which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: Her chance of spontaneous pregnancy within 6 months is clearly reduced.
options.why: In the Steiner (2017) cohort, a low AMH was not associated with a lower chance of conceiving in this population.

options.text: AMH alone does not predict her spontaneous conception; it would inform response if she ever needed stimulation.
options.why: Correct: it separates what AMH measures (follicle pool) from what it did not predict (fecundability).

options.text: She should start IVF immediately because of the low AMH.
options.why: AMH is not a fertility test: on its own it does not justify recommending IVF.

options.text: The low AMH indicates poorer oocyte quality.
options.why: AMH reflects follicle number; its relation to oocyte quality is weak or inconsistent.

items.explanation: What weighs in her plan is age, time trying and clinical assessment of the couple, not the AMH figure.

items.stem: In the Steiner et al. cohort (JAMA 2017), how was “conception” defined?

options.text: Live birth.
options.why: The study did not measure live births, so it cannot be extrapolated directly to that outcome.

options.text: Clinical pregnancy with heartbeat on ultrasound.
options.why: This was not the study outcome.

options.text: A positive pregnancy test.
options.why: Correct: an early outcome, different from clinical pregnancy and live birth.

options.text: Ongoing pregnancy at 12 weeks.
options.why: This was not the study outcome.

items.explanation: Reading the exact outcome is part of critical appraisal: biomarker, positive test, clinical pregnancy and live birth are not interchangeable.

items.stem: ESHRE (2023) states that, with regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to predict spontaneous conception. How is that recommendation graded?

options.text: Strong, with low certainty of evidence.
options.why: Correct: recommendation strength and evidence certainty are graded separately.

options.text: Strong, with high certainty.
options.why: The certainty assigned was low.

options.text: Conditional, with low certainty.
options.why: The recommendation is strong, not conditional.

options.text: Good practice point, no evidence.
options.why: It is an evidence-based recommendation with graded certainty.

items.explanation: A recommendation can be strong with low-certainty evidence when the balance of benefits, harms and costs is clear.

items.stem: A couple with an indication for IVF has an extremely low AMH. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Refuse IVF because there is no point trying.
options.why: ASRM: extremely low AMH values should not be used to refuse IVF.

options.text: Counsel on the expected response (fewer oocytes) and decide together, without using AMH as an exclusion criterion.
options.why: Correct: AMH informs counselling, not access.

options.text: Refer straight to egg donation without counselling on other options.
options.why: Using AMH to rule out treatment with her own oocytes without counselling amounts to denying access based on a marker, which ASRM advises against.

options.text: Do a clomiphene challenge test to confirm.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve accuracy and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: Reserve markers should not be used to deny access to infertility treatment.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with no current wish to conceive asks for an AMH “to decide whether to freeze my eggs”. What would you answer?

options.text: That if the AMH is low, she should freeze as soon as possible.
options.why: Reserve markers should not be used to promote planned freezing.

options.text: That AMH does not indicate who needs to freeze; the decision is discussed based on her reproductive plans and realistic information.
options.why: Correct: consistent with ASRM 2020.

options.text: That with a normal AMH she can postpone pregnancy without risk.
options.why: AMH does not predict reproductive potential; a normal AMH does not guarantee future fertility.

options.text: That a clomiphene challenge test in addition to AMH would help.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve accuracy and should be abandoned.

items.explanation: A low AMH does not mandate freezing, and a normal AMH does not make waiting risk-free.

items.stem: Regarding basal FSH as a marker of diminished ovarian reserve, which statement is correct?

options.text: It is sensitive: a normal FSH rules out low reserve.
options.why: It is not sensitive: a normal FSH does not rule it out.

options.text: It is specific but not sensitive.
options.why: Correct: if elevated it is informative, but if normal it does not rule out.

options.text: Its accuracy improves with a clomiphene challenge test.
options.why: Dynamic tests do not improve accuracy over basal markers.

options.text: It is the marker ESHRE recommends to predict response.
options.why: ESHRE recommends AFC or AMH, not basal FSH.

items.explanation: To estimate reserve when needed, AFC or AMH; isolated FSH does not rule out and the clomiphene test should be abandoned.

steps.text: Lucía (fictional case), 34, nulliparous, regular cycles. Her partner is 36. They have been trying for 5 months. A workplace check-up included an AMH reported as “low” by that laboratory's range. She is distressed and asks whether she should freeze her eggs or “go straight to IVF”.
First step: before interpreting the result, ask whether she was taking or recently stopped combined hormonal contraception, whether she had ovarian surgery, and which assay and cut-off the lab used.
Second step: explain what AMH measures (follicle number) and what it does not predict (spontaneous conception in women without known infertility).

Third step: AMH does not indicate that she should freeze or move to IVF. Per NICE, at 34 and without risk factors, investigations are offered after 1 year of unprotected intercourse; referral is brought forward from age 36 or if either partner has a known cause or predisposing factors.
Twist: months later, with a full work-up and an indication for IVF, AMH (or AFC) does help: it anticipates her response to stimulation and adjusts counselling, without being used to refuse treatment.
Communication: acknowledge her distress, explain the uncertainty honestly and avoid letting an isolated number become a diagnosis.

asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.title: Testing and interpreting measures of ovarian reserve: a committee opinion
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.population: Women with and without known infertility assessed with ovarian reserve markers.
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.finding: AMH and AFC predict oocyte yield in IVF well but are poor independent predictors of reproductive potential; they should not be used as a fertility test, to deny treatment, or to promote planned oocyte cryopreservation.
asrm-2020-ovarian-reserve.limitations: Committee opinion (not a GRADE guideline); US context.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.title: Ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI — ESHRE guideline update 2025
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Ovarian Stimulation
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.population: Women starting ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI.
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.finding: Recommends AFC or AMH to predict high and low response (strong). Does not recommend AFC, AMH or other basal markers to predict pregnancy or live birth (strong). Female age and BMI are predictors of pregnancy and live birth (strong). Age, BMI, FSH, inhibin B and other basal hormones should not be routinely used to predict response.
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.limitations: Full guideline v23 (September 2026); journal version: Hum Reprod 2026;41(4):498-514. Certainty for each recommendation is given in the full guideline.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

steiner-2017-jama.title: Association Between Biomarkers of Ovarian Reserve and Infertility Among Older Women of Reproductive Age
steiner-2017-jama.authors: Steiner AZ, Pritchard D, Stanczyk FZ, et al.
steiner-2017-jama.population: Prospective time-to-pregnancy cohort: women aged 30–44 with no history of infertility, trying to conceive for ≤3 months (North Carolina, USA); 981 enrolled, 750 analysed.
steiner-2017-jama.finding: AMH <0.7 ng/mL was not associated with a lower probability of conceiving by 6 cycles (65% vs 62%) or 12 cycles (84% vs 75%) versus normal AMH; neither was high FSH. Conception defined as a positive pregnancy test.
steiner-2017-jama.limitations: Outcome = positive pregnancy test, not live birth; observational; excludes known infertility; few women with very low AMH (n=84).

teede-2023-pcos-guideline.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.; International PCOS Network
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.finding: Graded recommendations (GRADE strength and certainty) on diagnosis (including AMH), glycaemic assessment, lifestyle, diet, metformin, inositol and ovulation induction with letrozole.
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.limitations: Many recommendations with low or very low certainty; practice points and consensus recommendations carry no certainty rating.
